title: The Adam–God doctrine: Brigham Young taught that Adam is God the Father
claim: On April 9, 1852, Brigham Young taught in general conference that Adam 'is our Father and our God, and the only God with whom we have to do' (Journal of Discourses 1:50–51). He repeated the teaching for over two decades — declaring in 1873 that 'Adam is my father' was doctrine God had revealed to him — and in 1877 had it incorporated into the temple lecture at the veil in the St. George Temple (L. John Nuttall journal, Feb. 7, 1877). The teaching contradicts Genesis (Adam is a creature formed by God, Gen 2:7), the Bible's insistence that God is not a man (Hosea 11:9), and canonized LDS scripture itself, which identifies Adam as the archangel Michael, subordinate to God (D&C 27:11; 107:53–55). In 1976 President Spencer W. Kimball told general conference: 'the Adam-God theory... We denounce that theory and hope that everyone will be cautioned against this and other kinds of false doctrine.' Either a prophet taught false doctrine over the pulpit and in the temple for 25 years, or the church now denounces true doctrine.

sources.name: MRM: 'Adam-God' — Brigham Young's Theory or Divine Doctrine?
Mormonr: Adam-God Theory (primary documents)
FAIR: Brigham Young and Adam-God theory
Institute for Religious Research: Adam-God Doctrine

response: FAIR argues that Young's sermons survive in imperfect transcriptions, that he elsewhere taught things inconsistent with a strong Adam–God reading, and that the teaching was never canonized by common consent — so it was a prophet's personal theological speculation, not church doctrine. Kimball's 1976 denunciation is presented as the system working: the living church self-corrects, and doctrine is defined by canonized scripture and the united voice of the First Presidency, not every pulpit statement of a past president.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Brigham Young and Adam-God theory

rationale: Kimball's 1976 denunciation concedes the substance: something Young taught as doctrine is now officially 'false doctrine.' The misreporting defense fails against multiple independent records — the Journal of Discourses, Young's own 1873 reaffirmation, Wilford Woodruff's journal, and the St. George temple lecture minutes. The remaining apologetic move ('never canonized') rescues the church's doctrinal process only by conceding the evangelistic point: a president of the church, speaking as prophet, taught for 25 years — including inside the temple — something the church now denounces, which collapses 'the prophet will never lead the church astray' as a working guarantee.

title: The priesthood restoration: no account of angelic ordination until 1834–35
claim: The church teaches that John the Baptist restored the Aaronic priesthood in May 1829 (D&C 13; JS–History 1:68–72) and Peter, James, and John the Melchizedek priesthood soon after. Yet no publication or record describes these angelic ordinations until Oliver Cowdery's October 1834 account in the Messenger and Advocate — five years later. Joseph's 1832 history does not narrate them; the 1833 Book of Commandments revelations contain none of the passages; and when the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants was prepared, the relevant text was added retroactively — what is now D&C 27 grew from a short 1830 revelation into one naming John the Baptist, Peter, James, and John (compare Book of Commandments 28). David Whitmer told interviewers he 'never heard that an Angel had ordained Joseph and Oliver to the Aaronic priesthood' until years after the church's 1830 organization, and William McLellin said the same. Critics conclude the restoration narrative developed after 1830 and was written back into the founding revelations.

sources.name: BYU Studies: Priesthood Restoration Documents
CES Letter: Priesthood Restoration
Joseph Smith Papers: Book of Commandments, 1833
FAIR: Response to CES Letter — Priesthood Restoration

response: FAIR and BYU scholars reply that Joseph's 1832 history does mention receiving 'the holy Priesthood by the ministring of Aangels,' that an 1829-era revelation (now D&C 27) alludes to authority from heavenly messengers, and that Joseph and Oliver kept the details private because of intense persecution — Joseph said they were 'forced to keep secret the circumstances of having received the Priesthood.' The 1835 expansions are framed as the prophet clarifying earlier revelations under the same inspiration, and Whitmer's and McLellin's recollections are dismissed as hostile memories recorded four to five decades later.
rationale: The documented facts favor the critics: the named-angel narrative appears nowhere before 1834, and the 1835 D&C additions are visible in the church's own Joseph Smith Papers. But the apologetic case is not empty — the 1832 history's 'ministring of Aangels' phrase and the persecution-secrecy argument are genuine (if ambiguous) counters, and late hostile recollections deserve discounting. What is beyond dispute is the retroactive textual expansion; what remains arguable is whether it records suppressed events or invents them. That split — solid textual evidence, live alternative explanation — is the definition of contested, though the pattern matches the First Vision's evolving accounts.

title: Revelations rewritten: the 1833 Book of Commandments vs. the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants
claim: Revelations published in 1833 as the direct word of God were materially rewritten for the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants — hundreds of changes, including substantive additions and reversals, all verifiable in the church's own Joseph Smith Papers scans. Examples: Book of Commandments 4:2 says God 'will grant him no other gift' than translating the Book of Mormon; D&C 5:4 rewrites this to 'no other gift until it is finished,' opening the door to Joseph's later revelatory career. BC 7 says Oliver Cowdery's gift is 'working with the rod' ('rod of nature'); D&C 8 renames the divining rod 'the gift of Aaron.' BC 28 (now D&C 27) grew from a short revelation into eighteen verses naming priesthood-restoring angels. Deuteronomy 4:2 and Proverbs 30:5–6 forbid adding to God's words; a 'thus saith the Lord' text that must be re-engineered years later to fit the movement's development looks like an evolving human composition, not delivered revelation.

sources.name: Joseph Smith Papers: Book of Commandments, 1833 (full scans)
IRR: Scanned images of the 1833 Book of Commandments and 1835 D&C
Tanner (UTLM): Changing the Revelations
LDS Discussions: Overview of Changes to the Revelations
FAIR: Doctrine and Covenants — Textual changes

response: FAIR argues Joseph Smith never claimed word-for-word divine dictation: revelations came as impressions expressed in his own imperfect language, so the prophet who received them had authority to revise, expand, and update them as church organization and his understanding grew — section 20's ecclesiastical additions simply incorporated offices revealed after 1830. The church publishes every version openly through the Joseph Smith Papers, which FAIR presents as the opposite of concealment, and the revised texts were accepted by common consent of the 1835 conference.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Doctrine and Covenants — Textual changes

rationale: The changes themselves are conceded and published by the church — the Joseph Smith Papers project puts both editions side by side, and FAIR's defense is a justification of the edits, not a denial of them. That satisfies 'admitted': the church's own publications concede the substance. The remaining dispute is interpretive — whether a prophet may revise God's words — and there the apologetic answer creates its own problem: if revelations are Joseph's fallible paraphrases subject to later re-engineering, the epistemic weight of any given 'thus saith the Lord' (including D&C 132) is correspondingly reduced. Severity is medium because the fact is damaging chiefly in combination with the priesthood-restoration backdating.

title: The 'Grammar and Alphabet of the Egyptian Language': Joseph Smith's translation method on paper
claim: Alongside the Book of Abraham 'translation,' Joseph Smith's circle produced the Kirtland Egyptian Papers, including a bound 'Grammar and Alphabet of the Egyptian Language' (1835, in the hands of W. W. Phelps and Warren Parrish, published in full by the Joseph Smith Papers). Joseph's own journal records him 'studying the Egyptian language' and that the group was 'engaged in translating an alphabet to the Book of Abraham, and arranging a grammar of the Egyptian language.' The system assigns single Egyptian characters paragraph-long English meanings that multiply through five 'degrees' — a scheme Egyptologists uniformly reject as bearing no relation to actual Egyptian. Three Book of Abraham manuscripts place characters copied sequentially from the recovered Hor Book of Breathings papyrus in the margins beside the English text. Unlike the gold plates, here the working papers of a Joseph Smith translation project survive — and they show a method that was not translation.

sources.name: Joseph Smith Papers: Grammar and Alphabet of the Egyptian Language (1835)
Wikipedia: Kirtland Egyptian papers
FAIR: What are the Kirtland Egyptian Papers and GAEL?
Pearl of Great Price Central: The Kirtland Egyptian Papers and the Book of Abraham

response: Apologists (Gee, Muhlestein, Pearl of Great Price Central) argue the direction of dependence is reversed: the Egyptian-language documents were the scribes' after-the-fact attempt to reverse-engineer Egyptian using the already-revealed English text, an intellectual exercise Joseph tolerated but did not author — most pages are in scribes' handwriting, the GAEL was never published or canonized, and textual evidence is argued to show the Abraham text preceding the Alphabet entries. On this view the KEP tell us about 1835 curiosity regarding Egyptian, not about how the Book of Abraham was produced.

responseSource.name: Pearl of Great Price Central: The Kirtland Egyptian Papers and the Book of Abraham

rationale: The narrow question — which came first, the English text or the Alphabet documents — is genuinely debated, with Joseph Smith Papers editors describing the documents as intertwined and scholars on both sides making textual arguments. So the strongest critical framing ('the GAEL was the translation engine') stays contested. But the apologetic escape is expensive: Joseph's own journal says he was arranging the grammar, and either direction leaves the prophet's circle producing, under his supervision, an 'Egyptian' system that is demonstrably nonsense. Paired with the papyri mismatch (covered separately), this is corroborating rather than standalone evidence — hence medium severity and a conservative contested grade.

title: Zelph: Joseph Smith identifies an Illinois skeleton as a 'white Lamanite' warrior
claim: On June 3, 1834, during Zion's Camp, Joseph Smith's men dug a skeleton with an arrowhead between its ribs from a burial mound near the Illinois River (Naples-Russell Mound 8, a Hopewell-culture site in Pike County, Illinois). According to diaries kept by at least six participants — Wilford Woodruff, Heber C. Kimball, George A. Smith, Levi Hancock, Moses Martin, Reuben McBride — Joseph declared by vision that the bones belonged to 'Zelph,' a 'white Lamanite' warrior-chieftain under 'the great prophet Onandagus,' killed in battle; several accounts say Onandagus was 'known from the Rocky Mountains to the eastern sea.' The story entered History of the Church 2:79–80. The episode shows Joseph exercising his revelatory gift on a checkable claim — a Hopewell burial unrelated to any Israelite civilization — and locating Book of Mormon peoples in North America, which limited Mesoamerican geography models must explain away.

sources.name: Kenneth Godfrey, 'The Zelph Story' (BYU Studies)
Wikipedia: Zelph
MormonThink: Zelph, ancient Mormon warrior
FAIR: Joseph Smith and Zelph

response: FAIR, drawing on Godfrey's source study, notes that Joseph himself wrote nothing about Zelph; the six diary accounts disagree on key details (which battle, whether the Rocky Mountains phrase was original), and the History of the Church version is a later scribal conflation that hardened a casual campfire comment into formal revelation. Even taken at face value, apologists argue Zelph could be a late-period Lamanite in the 'hinterlands' far from the Book of Mormon's core lands, so the story does not fix Book of Mormon geography.
rationale: The source-critical objections are real: the accounts genuinely diverge on details, and the canonical History version is a conflation — so the exact content of Joseph's statement is not recoverable with certainty, which keeps this out of 'unrefuted.' But all six independent diaries agree on the core: Joseph claimed a vision identifying a specific skeleton as a white Lamanite under a prophet named Onandagus. That core is either a false revelatory claim about a Hopewell burial or must be diluted to 'speculation' — the same unfalsifiability move seen elsewhere. Contested on the details, damaging on the pattern; medium severity.

title: Book of Mormon geography: from hemispheric certainty to official 'no position'
claim: For over a century the church taught a hemispheric Book of Mormon: canonized revelations identify North American Indians as Lamanites (D&C 28:8; 32:2; 54:8); Joseph Smith endorsed both Central American ruins (Times and Seasons, 1842) and North American sites ('plains of the Nephites,' Zelph) as Nephite; the New York hill where Joseph got the plates was officially Cumorah of the final battles (Mormon 6:6) — Joseph Fielding Smith warned the two-Cumorah theory would make members 'confused and disturbed in their faith,' and Marion Romney affirmed New York Cumorah in 1975 general conference. Under archaeological and DNA pressure, scholars retreated to limited-geography models; today the rival camps — Mesoamerican (FAIR, Scripture Central) and Heartland (Meldrum's FIRM Foundation) — each publish detailed refutations of the other. In 2019 the church's Gospel Topics statement declared it 'does not take a position on the specific geographic locations' and asked members not to teach any geography in church settings. No model reconciles the text, the founders' statements, and the evidence.

sources.name: Gospel Topics: Book of Mormon Geography
Wikipedia: Proposed Book of Mormon geographical setting
FAIR: Heartland Model of Book of Mormon geography (apologists vs. apologists)
LDS Discussions: Book of Mormon Geography (annotated essay)
Scripture Central: Church Releases Statement on Book of Mormon Geography

response: Apologists respond that the Book of Mormon text itself never names a modern location, and internal travel distances actually require a limited geography — so the hemispheric model was a cultural assumption early members (including Joseph, speaking as a man) layered onto the text, not revelation. Scripture Central argues a Mesoamerican setting satisfies dozens of textual criteria (writing systems, cities, warfare, demographics), and the church's official neutrality is appropriate humility on a question scripture leaves open, comparable to unresolved questions in biblical geography.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Heartland Model of Book of Mormon geography

rationale: The retreat itself is documented in the church's own statement, and the 'text never specifies' defense fails against canonized text: the D&C — scripture, not speculation — identifies specific North American tribes as Lamanites, and prophets taught New York Cumorah as doctrine. The strongest evidence that no answer works is the apologists themselves: FAIR and Scripture Central publish refutations of the Heartland model whose arguments (anachronism, distance, archaeology) mirror the critics' case against Mesoamerica, and vice versa. When every proposed location is convincingly refuted by fellow believers, the claim has become unfalsifiable by relocation. Medium severity because it is a meta-argument that leans on the archaeology and DNA entries.

title: Coercive proposals: the angel with a drawn sword and salvation-for-marriage promises
claim: The church's own Gospel Topics essay 'Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo' concedes that Joseph Smith told women an angel appeared three times commanding polygamy, and that in the final appearance 'the angel came with a drawn sword, threatening Joseph with destruction unless he went forward.' He deployed this account in proposals: to Zina Diantha Huntington (proposed to while she was courting Henry Jacobs; sealed to Joseph after being told of the angel; Henry later stood as witness), to Mary Elizabeth Rollins Lightner (already married), and to Lucy Walker, a 16-year-old living in his home after her mother's death, who was told to seek confirmation and later described her anguish. Helen Mar Kimball, 14, recorded Joseph's promise: 'If you will take this step, it will ensure your eternal salvation and exaltation, and that of your father's household.' D&C 132 canonizes the pattern: wives who refuse are 'destroyed' (vv. 54, 64). Scripture warns that even an angel preaching another gospel is accursed (Gal 1:8) and that Satan appears as an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14).

sources.name: Gospel Topics essay: Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo
Brian Hales: The Accounts of the Angel with a Drawn Sword
FAIR: Helen Mar Kimball — circumstances of her plural marriage
Christian Research Institute: Plural Marriage and Joseph Smith

response: Hales and FAIR argue the angel accounts originate with faithful participants and demonstrate Joseph's reluctance — he delayed for years and acted only under divine compulsion, the opposite of a predator's eagerness. They note Helen Mar Kimball's sealing was likely unconsummated and dynastic ('eternity-only'), linking families for the next life; that women like Sarah Pratt and Cordelia Morley refused Joseph without spiritual penalty, showing real agency; and that mid-19th-century marriage norms for young women differed sharply from today's, so modern coercion categories are anachronistic.

responseSource.name: Brian Hales: The Accounts of the Angel with a Drawn Sword

rationale: The essential facts are conceded in the church's own essay: the drawn-sword angel, Helen's marriage 'several months before her 15th birthday,' and sealings to already-married women. The salvation-promise to Helen is her own faithful memoir, and D&C 132's destruction threats are canon. The apologetic reframing (reluctance, dynastic sealings, era norms) disputes interpretation, not substance — and 'an angel threatened him into it' is itself the admission: the proposals bundled divine reward and divine threat, which is coercion by any biblical test, and Galatians 1:8 addresses precisely the scenario of angelic authorization for another gospel. High severity: it goes to the prophet's character and the fruit test.

title: Proxy baptism of Holocaust victims despite a signed agreement to stop
claim: LDS members performed proxy baptisms for hundreds of thousands of Holocaust victims. After Jewish organizations protested, the church signed a 1995 agreement to remove victims' names and stop the practice except for direct ancestors of members. Researcher Helen Radkey then repeatedly documented violations across two decades: Anne Frank's name submitted at least a dozen times and the ordinance performed at least nine times (including in the Santo Domingo Temple in February 2012, prompting a church condemnation); Simon Wiesenthal's parents baptized by proxy in early 2012, drawing a formal church apology to the family. The church revised its database controls in 2010 and threatened discipline for violators. The episode exposes the doctrine underneath: D&C 128:15 declares the dead 'cannot be made perfect' without our ordinances and that vicarious work is 'essential to our salvation' — resting on one disputed verse (1 Cor 15:29) against the Bible's teaching that judgment follows death (Heb 9:27) and that a fixed gulf separates the dead (Luke 16:26), a point the Book of Mormon itself makes (Alma 34:32–35).

sources.name: KSL: LDS Church issues statement after report of proxy baptism for Anne Frank
CBS News: Mormons apologize to Wiesenthal family for posthumous baptism
Fox 13: LDS Church condemns recent proxy baptism of Anne Frank
Mormonr: Holocaust Victims and Baptisms for the Dead

response: The church and Mormonr respond that proxy baptism compels no one — LDS doctrine holds the deceased may accept or reject the ordinance, so it is an offering, not a posthumous conversion; that the institution honored the 1995 agreement and each documented violation was the act of individual members contrary to explicit policy; and that the church responded seriously — removing names, engineering database blocks on Holocaust-victim submissions in 2010, apologizing to families, and warning that violators face loss of temple privileges or discipline.

responseSource.name: Mormonr: Holocaust Victims and Baptisms for the Dead

rationale: Every load-bearing fact is conceded by the church itself: the practice occurred, the 1995 agreement existed, violations continued for years, and the church publicly condemned and apologized for specific cases (Wiesenthal, Frank). The individual-members defense is fair as far as it goes but concedes the systemic point — a doctrine that makes ordinances for the dead 'essential to our salvation' generates relentless pressure that policy could not contain for two decades. The deeper evangelistic use is doctrinal: the entire temple-for-the-dead system hangs on 1 Corinthians 15:29 read against Hebrews 9:27, Luke 16:26, and even Alma 34. Medium severity.

title: Proposition 8: church-directed political mobilization for a state ballot measure
claim: In 2008 the First Presidency had a letter read from every California pulpit (June 29) urging members to 'do all you can' — 'your means and time' — to pass Proposition 8, which stripped same-sex marriage from California law. Ward and stake structures were converted into a precinct operation: assigned donation targets, phone banks, door-to-door canvassing coordinated with the Protect Marriage coalition the church joined at Catholic Archbishop Niederauer's invitation. Members contributed an estimated $20 million — roughly half the Yes campaign's funds — while Latter-day Saints were about 2% of Californians. The church itself reported in-kind contributions and was later fined by the California Fair Political Practices Commission for late-reported non-monetary contributions. This followed the same playbook used in Hawaii (1998) and California's Prop 22 (2000). The church's canonized position: 'We do not believe it just to mingle religious influence with civil government' (D&C 134:9). For evangelism, the point is institutional: a church claiming political neutrality directed member resources into civil law, then reversed course culturally within a decade (supporting the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act).

sources.name: Church Newsroom: Same-Sex Marriage and Proposition 8
Thomas Jefferson School of Law: An Overview of LDS Involvement in Prop 8
George Washington Law Review: Proposition 8 and the Mormon Church — A Case Study in Donor Disclosure
Religion Dispatches: When Mormons Mobilize
FAIR: Mormonism and politics — California Proposition 8

response: The church's Newsroom and FAIR respond that churches have always had the right — and a duty — to speak on moral questions, and marriage is a moral question, not partisan politics; the church endorsed no candidate or party. It joined a broad interfaith coalition (Catholics, evangelicals, Orthodox Jews, Muslims) rather than acting alone; direct institutional spending was a small, disclosed in-kind amount; members donated freely as private citizens; and D&C 134 also affirms that governments should protect the free exercise of conscience, which the church argues it was doing.

responseSource.name: Church Newsroom: Same-Sex Marriage and Proposition 8

rationale: The facts — the First Presidency letter, the coordinated fundraising through church channels, the dominant member share of campaign funds, the FPPC fine — are documented and not denied; the church's defense is a justification of its involvement, not a dispute of it. Graded admitted on the factual substance. Whether religious political advocacy is wrong is a judgment call Christians themselves divide over, so the entry's force for evangelism is narrower: the mismatch with D&C 134:9's canonized separation language, the pattern of mobilize-then-soften (Prop 8 to the 2015 POX to the 2019 reversal to Respect for Marriage), and what that pattern implies about 'revelation' tracking public pressure. Medium severity.

title: Huntsman v. LDS Church: the City Creek tithing-fraud suit
claim: In 2021 James Huntsman — of the prominent Huntsman family — sued the church for fraud, seeking the return of roughly $5 million in tithing. He cited President Hinckley's 2003 general conference assurance about the City Creek mall project: 'tithing funds have not and will not be used to acquire this property,' set against whistleblower David Nielsen's account that Ensign Peak Advisors — whose portfolio was built from surplus tithing — moved about $1.4 billion toward City Creek. A Ninth Circuit panel revived the claim in 2023, but on January 31, 2025, an 11-0 en banc court ruled for the church: six judges held no reasonable juror could find misrepresentation, because Hinckley in the same address said funds would come from 'commercial entities owned by the Church' and 'earnings of invested reserve funds'; the remaining judges would have barred the suit under the church-autonomy doctrine. The case matters as the highest-profile legal test of the church's tithing representations, adjacent to the SEC's separate $5M Ensign Peak settlement.

sources.name: Deseret News: Huntsman tithing lawsuit dismissed by unanimous 9th Circuit panel
Courthouse News: Church asks en banc Ninth Circuit to throw out fraud claims
Americans United: Huntsman v. Corporation of the President (case page)
Metropolitan News: Ninth Circuit judges disagree over why fraud suit fails
Sutherland Institute: Why the Ninth Circuit unanimously tossed the Huntsman lawsuit

response: The church's defense, accepted by the en banc majority, is that Hinckley's full 2003 statement distinguished tithing principal from 'earnings of invested reserve funds' and commercial-entity money, and City Creek was funded from the latter — so there was no misrepresentation, let alone fraud, and Huntsman produced no evidence tithing principal was spent. The concurring judges added that the First Amendment's church-autonomy doctrine forbids civil courts from adjudicating what a church told members about sacred donations at all.

responseSource.name: Sutherland Institute: Why the Ninth Circuit unanimously tossed the Huntsman lawsuit

rationale: After full adversarial testing, the fraud theory failed 11-0, and on the merits for a majority — not merely on constitutional avoidance. Hinckley's own contemporaneous wording anticipated the earnings-versus-principal distinction, so the residual complaint reduces to whether earnings on invested tithing are morally 'tithing,' a semantic and ethical quarrel rather than a demonstrated deception. Honest grading requires calling this answered; the church won this one. The broader transparency concern is real but belongs to the SEC/Ensign Peak entry, which stands on its own. Low severity: citing Huntsman as if it proved fraud would damage the evangelist's credibility.

title: Paul H. Dunn: a General Authority's fabricated faith-promoting stories
claim: Paul H. Dunn, a General Authority (Seventy, 1964–89) and one of the church's most beloved speakers, built talks and bestselling books on war and baseball stories that were fabricated: his best friend did not die in his arms in World War II, and he never played for the St. Louis Cardinals. Lynn Packer's investigation, published by the Arizona Republic in February 1991, documented the fabrications; Dunn initially defended them as necessary 'to illustrate his theological and moral points.' Church leaders had known years earlier — Packer's reporting was suppressed while Dunn was quietly given emeritus status in 1989 'for reasons of age and health.' In October 1991 Dunn published a confession in the Church News: 'I have not always been accurate in my public talks and writings,' acknowledging he had been censured by the First Presidency and the Twelve. The case is a documented instance of faith-promoting fabrication at the church's highest teaching level, and of the institution managing the image rather than the truth until forced.

sources.name: Deseret News (1991): Arizona paper alleges many stories were exaggerated
Deseret News (1991): Elder Dunn offers apology for errors, admits censure
Wikipedia: Paul H. Dunn
FAIR: Criticisms of Paul H. Dunn

response: FAIR responds that Dunn's dishonesty was personal failure, not church policy: the institution investigated, censured him, moved him to emeritus status, and required a public apology — evidence of accountability, not cover-up. Latter-day Saints do not claim their leaders are infallible or sinless; one man's embellished sermons say nothing about whether the Restoration is true, any more than a dishonest pastor disproves Protestantism. His apology and the church's acceptance of it model repentance.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Criticisms of Paul H. Dunn

rationale: Dunn's own published confession and admitted censure settle the facts; the church-owned Deseret News reported both. The apologetic point that one leader's sins don't falsify the religion is correct, which is why severity is low: this entry's value is as pattern evidence, not proof. What it legitimately illustrates is the ecology of 'faith-promoting' testimony — emotionally powerful stories generating spiritual witness in hearers who took that feeling as confirmation — and the institution's preference for quiet management (emeritus 'for age and health') over candor until journalism forced the issue. Use it to open the epistemology conversation, not as a standalone disproof.

title: The Mark Hofmann forgeries: prophets, seers, and undetected fraud
claim: From 1980–85 forger Mark Hofmann sold or donated to the church a stream of fake founding-era documents: the 'Anthon transcript' (1980), the Joseph Smith III blessing (1981, quietly traded to the RLDS church), and the 'salamander letter' (1984) in which 'Martin Harris' describes a white salamander, not an angel, guarding the plates — purchased for $40,000 by Steve Christensen and donated to the church. Senior leaders, including Gordon B. Hinckley, met Hofmann repeatedly and acquired sensitive items, some held in the First Presidency vault; leaders publicly downplayed what the church possessed. No apostle, seer, or revelator discerned the fraud. It unraveled only when Hofmann, fearing exposure, murdered Christensen and Kathy Sheets with pipe bombs in October 1985, and forensic examiner George Throckmorton proved the forgeries. The church's own history-topics essay now recounts the episode. The test: leaders sustained as 'seers' (D&C 46:23–27 promises the church discernment against deception) authenticated-by-acquisition documents attacking their own founding story rather than detecting a con man who later said he found deceiving the Brethren easy.

sources.name: Church History Topics: Hofmann Forgeries
Wikipedia: Salamander letter
Time: A Latter-Day Forger
FAIR: Church reaction to the Hofmann forgeries

response: FAIR responds that spiritual discernment is not omniscience: God does not shield leaders from ordinary human deception, and scripture shows prophets being deceived in mundane matters. The nation's best document examiners, dealers, and historians were equally fooled; the church bought documents as any archive acquires materials bearing on its history, published several of them (including the salamander letter) rather than suppressing them, and cooperated with prosecutors. Leaders' willingness to engage troubling documents is framed as openness, and Hofmann's success says something about forgery, nothing about revelation.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Church reaction to the Hofmann forgeries

rationale: The event sequence — meetings, purchases, the vault, the failure to detect, the murders — is conceded in the church's own essay; only significance is disputed. The 'discernment isn't omniscience' defense has force against a naive gotcha, but it prunes the claims of the office: D&C 46 promises discerning of spirits precisely 'lest ye be deceived,' and leaders' behavior — negotiating for and securing documents that undercut the founding narrative — showed they found a magic-salamander origin plausible enough to buy. That leaders treated the salamander letter as potentially authentic Martin Harris material is itself telling about the folk-magic milieu (covered in the seer-stone entry). Medium severity.

title: The burning in the bosom: Moroni 10:4 epistemology vs. the Bible's tests of truth
claim: The entire missionary system rests on Moroni 10:4–5: pray about the Book of Mormon and the Holy Ghost will confirm its truth — experienced as a feeling, the 'burning in the bosom' of D&C 9:8, which Dallin Oaks describes as 'a feeling of comfort and serenity.' Members are taught this witness outranks external evidence, and the confirmed feeling then validates the whole chain: book, prophet, priesthood, church. Two problems. First, the method cannot discriminate: Muslims, Catholics, evangelicals, and Strangites report equivalent confirming experiences for contradictory claims, so at most one set of feelings tracks truth. Second, Scripture commands the opposite order of testing: Deuteronomy 13:1–3 requires rejecting even a sign-working prophet whose doctrine is false; 'believe not every spirit, but try the spirits' (1 John 4:1); 'to the law and to the testimony' (Isaiah 8:20); the Bereans 'searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so' (Acts 17:11); and 'the heart is deceitful above all things' (Jeremiah 17:9). Biblically, doctrine tests experience — never the reverse.

sources.name: FAIR: Holy Ghost — Burning in the bosom
FAIR: Moroni's promise of the Book of Mormon
MormonThink: Mormon Testimony & Spiritual Witnesses
Midwest Christian Outreach: Examining the Faulty Logic of Moroni 10:4
wasmormon.org: Moroni's Promise and Begging the Question

response: FAIR argues personal revelation is thoroughly biblical: 'ask of God' (James 1:5), hearts burning on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:32), and Peter's testimony revealed 'not by flesh and blood' (Matthew 16:17). The witness is not raw emotion but knowledge borne by the Spirit, and D&C 9:8 commands study first — feeling confirms investigation rather than replacing it. Other faiths' spiritual experiences are expected, since God gives light to all people, and such experiences may soften hearts toward God generally without committing a person to a specific proposition; critics who reduce all spiritual experience to neurochemistry prove too much, undermining Christian conversion too.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Holy Ghost — Burning in the bosom

rationale: The apologetic defends that God can communicate — which the Christian gladly grants — but never answers the actual objection: how a feeling distinguishes true claims from false ones when contradictory religions produce identical feelings. FAIR's own concession that spiritual experiences may not 'commit one to a specific proposition' surrenders exactly the use Moroni 10:4 is put to, since the missionary program treats the feeling as certifying a very specific proposition set. And Deuteronomy 13:1–3 forecloses the move in principle: even genuine supernatural experience must yield to doctrinal testing. This is arguably the keystone entry — every other case in this app is waved off by appeal to the testimony this method produces. High severity.

title: Chiasmus in Alma 36: apologetic evidence examined
claim: The strongest literary argument for Book of Mormon antiquity: in 1969 John Welch identified extended chiasmus (inverted parallelism, A-B-C-C'-B'-A') in the Book of Mormon, with Alma 36 as the showpiece — a full-chapter structure pivoting on 'born of God' — argued to reflect an ancient Hebrew form Joseph Smith could not have known. The critical response, led by Earl Wunderli's 'Critique of Alma 36 as an Extended Chiasm' (Dialogue, 2005), shows Welch's outline depends on selective labeling: choosing some repeated words as structural elements while ignoring others that break the pattern, skipping intervening text, and tolerating loose matches — by Welch's own fifteen criteria the chapter scores poorly. Chiasm-like patterns also appear where no one claims Hebrew antiquity: in the Doctrine and Covenants and in ordinary 19th-century prose. Meanwhile chiasmus scholarship (e.g., John Jebb's 1820 'Sacred Literature') predated the Book of Mormon, though Smith's access is undemonstrated. Physicists Boyd and Farrell Edwards countered statistically that Alma 36's chiastic ordering is unlikely by chance; Wunderli rebutted their element selection.

sources.name: Earl Wunderli, 'Critique of Alma 36 as an Extended Chiasm' (Dialogue 38:4)
Boyd & Farrell Edwards, Response to Wunderli (Dialogue)
Wunderli, Response to the Edwardses (Dialogue)
Scholarly Publishing Collective: Critique of Alma 36 as an Extended Chiasm

response: The Edwardses' statistical analysis estimates a low probability that Alma 36's repeated elements would fall into chiastic order by chance, and argues their method does not depend on Welch's or Wunderli's contestable literary criteria. Apologists add that the structure is thematically apt — conversion at the center of an inverted life story — that candidate chiasms in the D&C are demonstrably weaker, and that there is no evidence Joseph Smith encountered Jebb or any chiasmus scholarship in rural New York before 1829.

responseSource.name: Boyd & Farrell Edwards, Response to Wunderli (Dialogue)

rationale: This is a genuine two-sided scholarly exchange in peer venues: Wunderli's selectivity critique lands, but the Edwardses' statistical reply is a serious counter that survives his rebuttal at least partially. Grading it contested — not dismissed — is both accurate and credibility-building. The deeper point for the evangelist: even granting a deliberate chiasm in Alma 36, the inference to antiquity fails independently — an author saturated in KJV parallelism could produce inverted structure, chiasmus appears in modern texts, and literary form cannot outweigh the anachronism, DNA, and textual evidence elsewhere in this app. Low severity: concede the phenomenon, contest the inference.

title: Nahom and the NHM altars: the strongest archaeological claim examined
claim: Apologists' flagship archaeological evidence: 1 Nephi 16:34 says Ishmael was buried 'in the place which was called Nahom' — a name the party did not coin — after which the group turned 'nearly eastward' (1 Nephi 17:1). Three limestone altars excavated from the Bar'an temple near Marib, Yemen (from 1988 on) carry dedications by a donor of the NHM (Nihm) tribe, dated to roughly the 7th–6th century BC — Lehi's era — and the Nihm tribal region lies near where the frankincense trail bends east toward the coast. Warren Aston and Scripture Central present this as a precise external hit. Critics respond: the inscriptions are three consonants naming a tribe, not a place called Nahom; the NHM root is common across Semitic names; the eastward turn matches incense-trail geography generally; and a form of the name ('Nehhm') appears on European maps from Carsten Niebuhr's expedition, in English by 1792 — so the correlation is explainable by common naming plus coincidence. Non-Mormon archaeologists attach no significance to the parallel (Philip Jenkins: 'there's no there there').

sources.name: Scripture Central: Book of Mormon Evidence — Nahom
Philip Jenkins: The Nahom Follies
MRM: Finding Nahom — The Continuing Search for Archaeological Confirmation
Ryan Thomas: Nahom and Lehi's Journey through Arabia, Part 3
FAIR: Possible locations for Nahom

response: Aston and Scripture Central argue NHM is rare as an Arabian toponym, that the altars independently anchor the tribal name to precisely Lehi's period and region — something unknowable from 1820s New York — and that no evidence connects Joseph Smith to Niebuhr's maps. They stress convergence: a burial place bearing a mourning-related Semitic root (NHM connotes consolation/mourning), positioned exactly where the text turns the party east, terminating at plausible 'Bountiful' candidates on the Omani coast — a chain of hits they argue multiplies well beyond coincidence.

responseSource.name: Scripture Central: Book of Mormon Evidence — Nahom

rationale: Honesty requires ranking this as the best single apologetic datum: a real inscriptional correlate, correctly dated, plausibly located. It is also far weaker than presented: a tribal name of three consonants, a root common in Semitic onomastics, a turn that follows the trade route everyone took, and a name available on published maps decades before 1829 — with academic archaeology outside Mormonism seeing nothing evidentiary in it. Both sides field serious arguments from real data, which is the definition of contested. For the evangelist: grant Nahom its full weight, then note that one consonant cluster in Arabia cannot offset the total absence of Nephite evidence in the New World, where the story's 1,000 years unfold.
